column1: What is the Liar sentence $L$ and why does it fail to admit a classical truth value?
column2: $L$ = 'This sentence is false.' Assuming $L$ is true forces $L$ to be false, and assuming $L$ is false forces $L$ to be true. Formally, $\tau(L) = \neg \tau(L)$, which has no solution in $\{\text{True}, \text{False}\}$.

column1: How does the Epimenides paradox differ structurally from the pure Liar paradox?
column2: Epimenides involves quantified self-reference over a class: $\forall x \in \text{Cretans}, \forall p \in \text{Statements}(x), \neg\tau(p)$. The contradiction arises only because Epimenides' own statement falls within the quantification domain, unlike the Liar's direct self-reference.

column1: What is Frege's Basic Law V, and why was it fatal to the Grundgesetze?
column2: Basic Law V states that the extension of concept $F$ equals the extension of concept $G$ iff $F$ and $G$ apply to exactly the same objects — equivalent to asserting $\{x \mid \varphi(x)\}$ exists for any predicate $\varphi$ (unrestricted comprehension). This permitted construction of the Russell set, deriving a contradiction and collapsing Frege's system.

column1: What is unrestricted comprehension, and what principle replaces it in axiomatic (Zermelo-Fraenkel) set theory?
column2: Unrestricted comprehension asserts that for any property $P$, the set of all things satisfying $P$ exists. ZF replaces this with restricted (separation/specification) comprehension: sets of elements satisfying $P$ can only be formed as subsets of an already-existing set, blocking self-referential paradoxical sets like Russell's.

column1: State Berry's Paradox and identify the metalinguistic predicate it exploits.
column2: 'The least natural number not describable in fewer than thirteen words' is itself a twelve-word description of that number — contradicting its own definition. It exploits unrestricted self-application of the predicate 'is describable in fewer than $n$ words' within the object language.

column1: What is the core mechanism exploited by Richard's Paradox?
column2: Richard's Paradox applies a diagonal enumeration to all real numbers definable in English, constructing a new real number (via diagonalization against the definable list) that is itself defined in English yet differs from every definable real on the list — a contradiction arising from treating 'definable in English' as a well-defined, enumerable predicate within the same language.

column1: What single architectural fault unites Berry's, Richard's, and König's paradoxes?
column2: Each embeds a metalinguistic predicate (definability, nameability, describability) directly into the object language and then applies that predicate self-referentially, conflating language and metalanguage to produce contradiction.

column1: Define the three structural components that decompose any logical paradox.
column2: (1) A referential substrate — the domain of objects/statements the paradox ranges over; (2) A closure principle — a rule for constructing new substrate members from conditions; (3) A negation/complement operation — enabling self-application in the negative mode, producing a fixed point.

column1: What is Invariant I (Consistency) in the resolution framework for paradoxes, and what does its loss imply under explosive logics?
column2: Consistency requires that the theory derives no formula $\varphi \wedge \neg\varphi$. Under explosive logics (validating ex falso quodlibet: $\varphi, \neg\varphi \vdash \psi$), losing consistency means every sentence becomes derivable, trivializing the entire consequence relation.

column1: What is Invariant II (Closure Completeness) and give its paradigmatic instance.
column2: Closure Completeness holds when the closure principle is unrestricted — every well-formed condition defines an object in the substrate. The paradigmatic instance is naive comprehension: 'for any predicate $\varphi$, there exists a class $\{x : \varphi(x)\}$,' which, together with Invariant I, is jointly unsatisfiable for self-referential substrates (the core impossibility relation among the resolution invariants).
